story.title: UN Experts Warn US Deportations Lead to Rights Abuses
story.summary: Independent UN experts have raised concerns that US deportation policies are causing a 'cascade' of human rights abuses, including risks of torture and enforced disappearance. Reports indicate that over 25,000 third-country nationals have been deported, with the US having agreements with more than 35 countries.

explore_lenses.label: Why do third-country removals matter?
explore_lenses.title: The dispute is about safety screening, not just destination
explore_lenses.summary: A removal order can sometimes be executed through a country other than a person’s homeland, but protections against persecution or torture still apply to the proposed destination. UN experts argue the current arrangements risk bypassing those protections for people with no meaningful connection to the receiving country.

claims.text: The Justice Department states that a person granted withholding of removal cannot be sent to the country where their life or freedom would be threatened, but may be removed to a third country where those risks are absent.

The UN experts’ position is that transfer and receiving states retain human-rights obligations, including non-refoulement protections, even when removals are arranged through bilateral deals or diplomatic assurances.

The experts say risks extend beyond direct return to a home country: deportees may face detention, trafficking, discrimination, or onward removal from a destination lacking asylum procedures and durable support.

explore_lenses.label: Why is the US using third countries?
explore_lenses.title: It is a tool for cases blocked from direct return
explore_lenses.summary: The administration has presented third-country removal as a way to execute final removal orders when direct repatriation is unavailable or barred. Critics say the policy’s rapid procedures and limited transparency make it difficult for affected people to contest danger in the new destination.

claims.text: Administration officials have said third-country removals are needed for some people with final removal orders who cannot be returned to their home countries because of protection orders or because those governments will not accept them.

The First Circuit described the challenged 2025 DHS guidance as covering removals to countries neither named in the removal order nor previously identified in writing during the person’s immigration proceedings.

A Forbidden Stories-led investigation reported at least 25,447 third-country removals through August 31, 2026, with about 20,000 involving Mexico; the count is based on compiled and cross-checked reporting data rather than a comprehensive US government release.

explore_lenses.label: What could change after the court ruling?
explore_lenses.title: The policy faces a due-process constraint
explore_lenses.summary: On September 18, 2026, the First Circuit largely upheld a ruling against DHS’s streamlined third-country-removal guidance. The decision does not categorically prohibit all such removals, but it requires meaningful notice and an opportunity to raise destination-specific fears of persecution or torture.

claims.text: The First Circuit affirmed the judgment that DHS’s guidance was unlawful, while vacating only the separate part of the lower-court ruling that required DHS first to seek removal to a designated or nationality country.
The court held that the government’s procedures must give affected noncitizens effective notice and a meaningful opportunity to present fear-based objections before removal to a third country.

Forecast: legal experts told The Washington Post that the administration is likely to seek Supreme Court review and a stay, which could determine whether removals continue under modified procedures while the case proceeds.

story_report.summary: Independent UN experts warned that U.S. deportations to third countries are creating heightened risks of torture and ill-treatment, describing a broader cascade of potential rights abuses. More than 25,000 third-country nationals had been removed by the end of August, under arrangements involving more than 35 countries. The warning adds international human-rights scrutiny to a policy that a federal appeals court has found unlawful in its challenged form, requiring meaningful procedural protections before such removals.

sections.heading: Third-country removal policy rationale
sections.body: Justice Department guidance says a person granted withholding of removal cannot be sent to a country where their life or freedom would be threatened, but may be sent to a third country where those risks are absent. Administration officials have said such removals are necessary for some people with final removal orders whose home countries will not accept them or who cannot be returned there because of protection orders. The challenged 2025 DHS guidance covered destinations not named in removal orders or previously identified in writing during immigration proceedings.

sections.heading: UN experts cite onward-transfer risks
sections.body: The UN experts say transfer and receiving countries retain human-rights duties, including non-refoulement protections, even when removals are arranged through bilateral deals or diplomatic assurances. In their assessment, risks can extend beyond a direct return to a person’s home country: deportees may face detention, trafficking, discrimination or onward removal after arrival in countries without asylum procedures or durable support. Their statement assesses risks and legal obligations rather than establishing abuse in every individual transfer.

sections.heading: Appeals court requires procedural safeguards
sections.body: The First Circuit affirmed a judgment that DHS guidance governing the removals was unlawful, though it vacated the separate requirement that DHS first seek removal to a designated or nationality country. The court held that noncitizens must receive effective notice and a meaningful opportunity to raise fear-based objections before removal to a third country. Legal experts told The Washington Post the administration was likely to seek Supreme Court review and a stay, which could affect whether removals continue under revised procedures.

unresolved.text: The complete scope and terms of country-specific deportation arrangements remain unclear because many agreements and transfers have not been publicly detailed by the U.S. government.
As of Sept. 28, 2026, it remained unresolved whether the administration would seek Supreme Court intervention, whether a stay would be granted, and what revised DHS procedures would require.

related_stories.title: Taylor Swift Makes History at MTV VMAs, Dedicates Award to Dolly Parton
related_stories.summary: At the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards, Taylor Swift became the most-awarded artist in the event's history. She dedicated her top prize, Video of the Year for 'The Fate of Ophelia,' to Dolly Parton, who was honored during the ceremony. Madonna also had a notable night, winning multiple awards, including Artist of the Year.

related_stories.summary: On Sunday, September 27, London’s Southwark Bridge was transformed into a lively scene as the annual Woolmen’s Sheep Drive took place. The event featured sheep parading across the bridge, drawing attention and participation from the public.

related_stories.title: SpaceX's Starship Achieves First Orbital Flight
related_stories.summary: SpaceX's Starship successfully reached orbit for the first time during its 14th test flight, marking a significant milestone for the company and NASA. The mission, which launched from Texas, is crucial for future plans to land humans on the moon and beyond. However, the test flight concluded earlier than anticipated.
